VaR, expected shortfall, and tail uncertainty

A loss quantile specifies a threshold. Expected shortfall averages the losses in an upper probability slice. Both depend on a probability law; reporting either quantity without its model and estimation assumptions leaves the uncertainty unresolved.

SCoFT v4, chapter 13, §13.3, pp. 257–258 Taleb, 2025, motivates the error-propagation question. Its random-probability calculation is derived in probability conflation. Here we define the risk measures precisely and prove additional results for a random Pareto exponent. These two uncertainty models are distinct.

Quantiles and expected shortfall¶

Let X≥0X\ge0X≥0 be a finite almost surely loss, with CDF FFF and survival Fˉ\bar FFˉ as in the notation canon. Use 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1 for confidence and p=1−τp=1-\taup=1−τ for tail mass; α\alphaα remains the tail exponent. Define

qτ=inf⁡{x:F(x)≥τ},VaR⁡τ(X)=qτ,ES⁡τ(X)=1p∫τ1qs ds.\begin{gathered} q_\tau=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge\tau\},\\ \operatorname{VaR}_\tau(X)=q_\tau,\\ \operatorname{ES}_\tau(X) =\frac1p\int_\tau^1 q_s\,ds. \end{gathered}qτ​=inf{x:F(x)≥τ},VaRτ​(X)=qτ​,ESτ​(X)=p1​∫τ1​qs​ds.​
(1)

The quantile is finite for each interior confidence level. The integral may be infinite. ES selects the upper mass ppp, including the required fraction of an atom at the quantile. Consequently the strict conditional mean E[X∣X>qτ]\mathbb E[X\mid X>q_\tau]E[X∣X>qτ​] is not a general definition of ES.

We prove the equivalent excess-payoff formula, which also handles atoms.

Proposition 1 (Expected shortfall as a quantile plus expected excess)

Let X≥0X\ge0X≥0 be finite almost surely, let 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1 and p=1−τp=1-\taup=1−τ, and let qs=inf⁡{x:F(x)≥s}q_s=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge s\}qs​=inf{x:F(x)≥s} for its CDF FFF. The quantile-defined ES⁡τ(X)=p−1∫τ1qs ds\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)=p^{-1}\int_\tau^1q_s\,dsESτ​(X)=p−1∫τ1​qs​ds satisfies

E[(X−qτ)+]=∫τ1(qs−qτ) ds,ES⁡τ(X)=qτ+E[(X−qτ)+]p.\begin{gathered} \mathbb E[(X-q_\tau)_+]=\int_\tau^1(q_s-q_\tau)\,ds,\\ \operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)=q_\tau+\frac{\mathbb E[(X-q_\tau)_+]}p. \end{gathered}E[(X−qτ​)+​]=∫τ1​(qs​−qτ​)ds,ESτ​(X)=qτ​+pE[(X−qτ​)+​]​.​
(2)

These identities hold in the extended nonnegative reals. The atom correction is

pES⁡τ(X)=E[X1{X>qτ}]+qτ{p−P(X>qτ)}.\begin{aligned} p\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X) &=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>q_\tau\}}]\\ &\quad+q_\tau\{p-P(X>q_\tau)\}. \end{aligned}pESτ​(X)​=E[X1{X>qτ​}​]+qτ​{p−P(X>qτ​)}.​
(3)

If P(X>qτ)=pP(X>q_\tau)=pP(X>qτ​)=p, then ES⁡τ(X)=E[X∣X>qτ]\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)=\mathbb E[X\mid X>q_\tau]ESτ​(X)=E[X∣X>qτ​].

Proof 1

Represent the loss by its quantile function evaluated at a uniform random variable; this has CDF FFF. Monotonicity gives qs≤qτq_s\le q_\tauqs​≤qτ​ below τ\tauτ and qs≥qτq_s\ge q_\tauqs​≥qτ​ above τ\tauτ. Hence E[(X−qτ)+]=∫τ1(qs−qτ) ds\mathbb E[(X-q_\tau)_+]=\int_\tau^1(q_s-q_\tau)\,dsE[(X−qτ​)+​]=∫τ1​(qs​−qτ​)ds. Adding pqτpq_\taupqτ​ proves the excess formula, including infinite integrals. The identity (X−qτ)+=X1{X>qτ}−qτ1{X>qτ}(X-q_\tau)_+=X\mathbf1_{\{X>q_\tau\}}-q_\tau\mathbf1_{\{X>q_\tau\}}(X−qτ​)+​=X1{X>qτ​}​−qτ​1{X>qτ​}​ gives the atom correction. When P(X>qτ)=pP(X>q_\tau)=pP(X>qτ​)=p, the correction vanishes and division by p>0p>0p>0 gives the conditional mean.

For a law continuous at qτq_\tauqτ​, P(X>qτ)=pP(X>q_\tau)=pP(X>qτ​)=p. The unconditional tail-level quantity from the calibration note is then E[X1{X>qτ}]=pES⁡τ(X)\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>q_\tau\}}]=p\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)E[X1{X>qτ​}​]=pESτ​(X), not ES itself.

Use discrete_risk. Here the worst tenth of the law includes all the losses of 20 and some losses of 5. Averaging only observations strictly above the quantile would give a different answer.

from xmath.incerto.risk_measures import discrete_risk

risk = discrete_risk([0, 5, 20], [.85, .1, .05], .1)
print(f"VaR={risk['var']:.1f}, ES={risk['es']:.1f}")

Output

VaR=5.0, ES=12.5

VaR is also a minimizer of expected quantile loss when the first moment is finite, as proved in the point-forecast note. Use quantile_loss and finite_payoff_mean to compare three candidate thresholds under this same finite law.

from xmath.incerto.forecasting import quantile_loss
from xmath.incerto.lecture_risk import finite_payoff_mean

for threshold in (0, 5, 20):
    losses = quantile_loss([0, 5, 20], threshold, tau=.9)
    risk = finite_payoff_mean([.85, .1, .05], losses)
    print(f"threshold={threshold}: expected quantile loss={risk:.2f}")

Output

threshold=0: expected quantile loss=1.35
threshold=5: expected quantile loss=1.10
threshold=20: expected quantile loss=1.85

A quantile can fail subadditivity¶

Proposition 2 (A finite counterexample to VaR subadditivity)

Suppose (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y) takes (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) with probability 0.92, (10,0)(10,0)(10,0) with probability 0.04, and (0,10)(0,10)(0,10) with probability 0.04. At confidence 0.95, each marginal has VaR zero, while X+YX+YX+Y has VaR 10, so VaR⁡0.95(X+Y)>VaR⁡0.95(X)+VaR⁡0.95(Y)\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X+Y)> \operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(X)+\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(Y)VaR0.95​(X+Y)>VaR0.95​(X)+VaR0.95​(Y).

Proof 2

Each marginal has mass 0.96 at zero. The sum has mass 0.92 at zero and 0.08 at ten, so its CDF first reaches 0.95 at ten.

This is not a claim that every portfolio violates subadditivity.

The quantile definition also applies to real integrable losses. On that domain, ES is subadditive regardless of dependence. We prove this from the excess formula.

Lemma 1 (Expected shortfall minimizes an excess-payoff objective)

For a real random variable XXX with E∣X∣<∞\mathbb E|X|<\inftyE∣X∣<∞, fix 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1 and p=1−τp=1-\taup=1−τ. Define its quantiles qsq_sqs​ and ES by the same quantile formulas above, and for t∈Rt\in\mathbb Rt∈R let

JX(t)=t+E[(X−t)+]p.J_X(t)=t+\frac{\mathbb E[(X-t)_+]}p.JX​(t)=t+pE[(X−t)+​]​.
(4)

Then ES⁡τ(X)=min⁡t∈RJX(t)=JX(qτ)\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)=\min_{t\in\mathbb R}J_X(t)=J_X(q_\tau)ESτ​(X)=mint∈R​JX​(t)=JX​(qτ​).

Proof 3

Integrating qs−t≤(qs−t)+q_s-t\le(q_s-t)_+qs​−t≤(qs​−t)+​ over the upper slice gives ES⁡τ(X)≤JX(t)\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)\le J_X(t)ESτ​(X)≤JX​(t). Equality holds at t=qτt=q_\taut=qτ​ by the quantile argument in Proposition 1, which also applies to real integrable XXX: all relevant integrals are finite.

Proposition 3 (Expected shortfall is subadditive)

Let X,YX,YX,Y be real random variables on the same probability space with E∣X∣+E∣Y∣<∞\mathbb E|X|+\mathbb E|Y|<\inftyE∣X∣+E∣Y∣<∞, under arbitrary dependence. For every 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1,

ES⁡τ(X+Y)≤ES⁡τ(X)+ES⁡τ(Y).\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X+Y) \le\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)+\operatorname{ES}_\tau(Y).ESτ​(X+Y)≤ESτ​(X)+ESτ​(Y).
(5)
Proof 4

Use the objectives in Lemma 1. The pointwise inequality

(X+Y−t−s)+≤(X−t)++(Y−s)+(X+Y-t-s)_+ \le(X-t)_++(Y-s)_+(X+Y−t−s)+​≤(X−t)+​+(Y−s)+​
(6)

implies JX+Y(t+s)≤JX(t)+JY(s)J_{X+Y}(t+s)\le J_X(t)+J_Y(s)JX+Y​(t+s)≤JX​(t)+JY​(s). Choose marginal quantile minimizers and minimize the left side to obtain

ES⁡τ(X+Y)≤ES⁡τ(X)+ES⁡τ(Y).\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X+Y) \le\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)+\operatorname{ES}_\tau(Y).ESτ​(X+Y)≤ESτ​(X)+ESτ​(Y).
(7)
Proposition 4 (Order, scale, and translation properties of expected shortfall)

Fix 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1. For integrable real losses X,YX,YX,Y, X≤YX\le YX≤Y almost surely implies ES⁡τ(X)≤ES⁡τ(Y)\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)\le\operatorname{ES}_\tau(Y)ESτ​(X)≤ESτ​(Y). For c≥0c\ge0c≥0 and b∈Rb\in\mathbb Rb∈R, ES⁡τ(cX)=cES⁡τ(X)\operatorname{ES}_\tau(cX)=c\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)ESτ​(cX)=cESτ​(X) and ES⁡τ(X+b)=ES⁡τ(X)+b\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X+b)=\operatorname{ES}_\tau(X)+bESτ​(X+b)=ESτ​(X)+b.

Proof 5

Almost-sure order implies the same order of quantiles. Positive scaling scales every quantile, and translation adds bbb to every quantile. Integrate these identities over the upper slice; the case c=0c=0c=0 is the constant zero law.

These properties explain the coherence of ES. They do not bound the sampling error of an estimated ES, nor make an infinite ES finite.

from xmath.incerto.risk_measures import discrete_risk

for name, x in (("X", [0, 10, 0]), ("Y", [0, 0, 10]), ("X+Y", [0, 10, 10])):
    r = discrete_risk(x, [.92, .04, .04], .05)
    print(f"{name}: VaR={r['var']:.1f}, ES={r['es']:.1f}")

Output

X: VaR=0.0, ES=8.0
Y: VaR=0.0, ES=8.0
X+Y: VaR=10.0, ES=10.0

Exact Pareto risk and its moment boundary¶

Proposition 5 (Pareto VaR and expected shortfall)

For X∼Pareto⁡(α,xm)X\sim\operatorname{Pareto}(\alpha,x_m)X∼Pareto(α,xm​) with α>0\alpha>0α>0, xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, fix 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1 and p=1−τp=1-\taup=1−τ. Then

qτ=xmp−1/α,ES⁡τ(X)=αα−1qτ,α>1.\begin{gathered} q_\tau=x_m p^{-1/\alpha},\\ \operatorname{ES}_\tau(X) =\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}q_\tau,\\ \alpha>1. \end{gathered}qτ​=xm​p−1/α,ESτ​(X)=α−1α​qτ​,α>1.​
(8)

For 0<α≤10<\alpha\le10<α≤1, ES is infinite at every such confidence level, while VaR remains finite.

Proof 6

Invert Fˉ(x)=(xm/x)α\bar F(x)=(x_m/x)^\alphaFˉ(x)=(xm​/x)α to get qτq_\tauqτ​. For α>1\alpha>1α>1, integrate the Pareto survival above qτq_\tauqτ​: E[(X−qτ)+]=pqτ/(α−1)\mathbb E[(X-q_\tau)_+]=pq_\tau/(\alpha-1)E[(X−qτ​)+​]=pqτ​/(α−1), then substitute into the excess formula. For 0<α≤10<\alpha\le10<α≤1 this integral diverges, hence ES is infinite at every interior confidence level, while VaR remains finite.

These are exact-Pareto statements. The equality case for a general regularly varying law can depend on its slowly varying factor; see moment existence.

Use pareto_risk.

from xmath.incerto.risk_measures import pareto_risk

for alpha in (.8, 1, 1.2, 2, 3):
    r = pareto_risk(alpha, .01)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:g}: VaR={r['var']:.2f}, ES={r['es']:.2f}")

Output

alpha=0.8: VaR=316.23, ES=inf
alpha=1: VaR=100.00, ES=inf
alpha=1.2: VaR=46.42, ES=278.50
alpha=2: VaR=10.00, ES=20.00
alpha=3: VaR=4.64, ES=6.96

Random exponents: averaging model risk¶

Hold the cutoff xmx_mxm​ and tail mass p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1)p∈(0,1) fixed. View the quantile as a function of the exponent.

Proposition 6 (Convexity of Pareto model risk in the exponent)

Fix xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1)p∈(0,1). The function v(a)=xmp−1/av(a)=x_m p^{-1/a}v(a)=xm​p−1/a is decreasing and strictly convex on a>0a>0a>0, and h(a)=av(a)/(a−1)h(a)=a v(a)/(a-1)h(a)=av(a)/(a−1) is strictly convex on a>1a>1a>1. For a positive random exponent AAA with finite mean a0a_0a0​, Ev(A)≥v(a0)\mathbb E v(A)\ge v(a_0)Ev(A)≥v(a0​). If also A>1A>1A>1 almost surely, then Eh(A)≥h(a0)\mathbb E h(A)\ge h(a_0)Eh(A)≥h(a0​). Each inequality allows an infinite left side, and equality holds exactly when AAA is almost surely constant.

Proof 7

Since log⁡p<0\log p<0logp<0, direct differentiation gives

v′(a)=log⁡pa2v(a),v′′(a)v(a)=−2log⁡pa3+(log⁡p)2a4>0.\begin{gathered} v'(a)=\frac{\log p}{a^2}v(a),\\ \frac{v''(a)}{v(a)}=-\frac{2\log p}{a^3}+\frac{(\log p)^2}{a^4}>0. \end{gathered}v′(a)=a2logp​v(a),v(a)v′′(a)​=−a32logp​+a4(logp)2​>0.​
(9)

Thus vvv is decreasing and strictly convex.

For a>1a>1a>1, the model ES is h(a)=av(a)/(a−1)h(a)=a v(a)/(a-1)h(a)=av(a)/(a−1). Its curvature follows by logarithmic differentiation:

(log⁡h)′(a)=−1a(a−1)+log⁡pa2,(log⁡h)′′(a)=2a−1a2(a−1)2−2log⁡pa3>0,h′′(a)=h(a){(log⁡h)′′(a)+[(log⁡h)′(a)]2}>0.\begin{gathered} (\log h)'(a)=-\frac1{a(a-1)}+\frac{\log p}{a^2},\\ (\log h)''(a)=\frac{2a-1}{a^2(a-1)^2}-\frac{2\log p}{a^3}>0,\\ h''(a)=h(a)\bigl\{(\log h)''(a)+[(\log h)'(a)]^2\bigr\}>0. \end{gathered}(logh)′(a)=−a(a−1)1​+a2logp​,(logh)′′(a)=a2(a−1)22a−1​−a32logp​>0,h′′(a)=h(a){(logh)′′(a)+[(logh)′(a)]2}>0.​
(10)

Therefore averaging model ES is at least ES at the mean exponent when A>1A>1A>1 almost surely and EA<∞\mathbb E A<\inftyEA<∞, with equality exactly when AAA is almost surely constant. The same Jensen argument applies to vvv. In either case, the tangent at a0a_0a0​ has an integrable affine part and a nonnegative remainder, strictly positive away from a0a_0a0​; this justifies Jensen and its equality condition even if the expectation is infinite.

This averages the quantiles or ES of conditional models. It does not yet compute predictive mixture risk, and it is not a bias claim about an arbitrary estimator: if AAA represents an estimator, its mean need not equal the true exponent.

Proposition 7 (Finite component shortfalls can have an infinite average)

Fix xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1)p∈(0,1), and let h(a)=axmp−1/a/(a−1)h(a)=a x_m p^{-1/a}/(a-1)h(a)=axm​p−1/a/(a−1) for a>1a>1a>1, extended by infinity for 0<a≤10<a\le10<a≤1. If AAA is uniform on (1,2)(1,2)(1,2), every component ES is finite but Eh(A)=∞\mathbb E h(A)=\inftyEh(A)=∞. For any positive random AAA with P(A≤1)>0P(A\le1)>0P(A≤1)>0, the average is also infinite.

Proof 8

For the uniform case, h(a)≥xm/(a−1)h(a)\ge x_m/(a-1)h(a)≥xm​/(a−1) on (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) and the integral of this lower bound diverges. In the second case, h(A)=∞h(A)=\inftyh(A)=∞ on an event of positive probability.

Proposition 8 (Small bounded perturbations of the Pareto exponent)

Fix xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1)p∈(0,1). Let f(a)=xmp−1/af(a)=x_m p^{-1/a}f(a)=xm​p−1/a on a>0a>0a>0 or f(a)=axmp−1/a/(a−1)f(a)=a x_m p^{-1/a}/(a-1)f(a)=axm​p−1/a/(a−1) on a>1a>1a>1. Take a0a_0a0​ in the chosen domain and a bounded random variable ZZZ with EZ=0\mathbb E Z=0EZ=0. For A=a0+εZA=a_0+\varepsilon ZA=a0​+εZ and ε→0\varepsilon\to0ε→0 small enough that AAA stays in a fixed compact interval inside that domain,

Ef(A)−f(a0)=12ε2f′′(a0)EZ2+O(ε3).\begin{aligned} \mathbb E f(A)-f(a_0) &=\tfrac12\varepsilon^2f''(a_0)\mathbb E Z^2\\ &\quad+O(\varepsilon^3). \end{aligned}Ef(A)−f(a0​)​=21​ε2f′′(a0​)EZ2+O(ε3).​
(11)
Proof 9

Taylor-expand f(a0+εZ)f(a_0+\varepsilon Z)f(a0​+εZ) through second order and take expectations. The linear term vanishes because EZ=0\mathbb E Z=0EZ=0. The third derivative is bounded on the compact interval. The remainder is bounded by a constant times ∣ε∣3E∣Z∣3|\varepsilon|^3\mathbb E|Z|^3∣ε∣3E∣Z∣3.

The ES expansion needs a0>1a_0>1a0​>1 and a perturbation that stays above one. A variance alone, without these support and remainder conditions, does not justify the approximation. For comparisons between two uncertainty laws, convex order is sufficient; larger variance alone is not.

Mixing distributions is a different operation¶

Proposition 9 (Common-cutoff exponent mixtures dominate the mean-exponent law)

Specify X∣A∼Pareto⁡(A,xm)X\mid A\sim\operatorname{Pareto}(A,x_m)X∣A∼Pareto(A,xm​) with the same fixed xmx_mxm​ in every component, A>0A>0A>0 almost surely, and finite a0=EAa_0=\mathbb E Aa0​=EA, where xm>0x_m>0xm​>0. For x>xmx>x_mx>xm​,

Fˉmix(x)=E[(xm/x)A],Fˉmix(x)≥(xm/x)a0.\begin{gathered} \bar F_{\rm mix}(x)=\mathbb E[(x_m/x)^A],\\ \bar F_{\rm mix}(x)\ge(x_m/x)^{a_0}. \end{gathered}Fˉmix​(x)=E[(xm​/x)A],Fˉmix​(x)≥(xm​/x)a0​.​
(12)

The mixture has finite quantiles at every interior confidence level, each at least the corresponding quantile of the Pareto law with exponent a0a_0a0​, and strictly larger if AAA is nonconstant. Its ES is also at least that of the mean-exponent law, allowing infinity.

Proof 10

Condition on AAA for the survival formula and apply Jensen to a↦(xm/x)aa\mapsto(x_m/x)^aa↦(xm​/x)a, a strictly convex function for x>xmx>x_mx>xm​. This gives first-order stochastic dominance and hence the quantile order. Dominated convergence makes the mixture survival continuous, with value one at xmx_mxm​ and limit zero at infinity. It is strictly decreasing because every component survival is. Strict Jensen therefore implies strict quantile order for nonconstant AAA. Integrating quantiles gives the ES order.

The inequality is specific to this common-cutoff exponent mixture. Holding a median or mean fixed by changing xmx_mxm​ is a different comparison.

Proposition 10 (Finite mixture quantiles with infinite averaged risk)

Fix xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and let X∣A∼Pareto⁡(A,xm)X\mid A\sim\operatorname{Pareto}(A,x_m)X∣A∼Pareto(A,xm​). If AAA is uniform on (1,2)(1,2)(1,2), the mixture mean and ES are infinite, while its VaR is finite at every 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1. If AAA is uniform on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), then for every p=1−τ∈(0,1)p=1-\tau\in(0,1)p=1−τ∈(0,1), the average model VaR E[xmp−1/A]\mathbb E[x_m p^{-1/A}]E[xm​p−1/A] is infinite while the mixture VaR remains finite.

Proof 11

Finite mixture quantiles follow from Proposition 9. With AAA uniform on (1,2)(1,2)(1,2), Tonelli gives an infinite mixture mean, hence infinite ES; truncating the loss below any finite quantile cannot remove that infinite tail mean. Explicitly, E[X∣A]=xmA/(A−1)≥xm/(A−1)\mathbb E[X\mid A]=x_m A/(A-1)\ge x_m/(A-1)E[X∣A]=xm​A/(A−1)≥xm​/(A−1) has divergent integral.

With AAA uniform on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), E[p−1/A]=∞\mathbb E[p^{-1/A}]=\inftyE[p−1/A]=∞ for every 0<p<10<p<10<p<1. This follows by substituting z=1/Az=1/Az=1/A: the resulting integral of p−z/z2p^{-z}/z^2p−z/z2 diverges.

No identity interchanges averaging a quantile with mixing laws.

Use pareto_mixture_risk for the predictive mixture and pareto_risk for components. The two exponents below have mean two. The mixture ES is evaluated at its own quantile, not at either component quantile.

Compare three risk calculations
from xmath.incerto.risk_measures import pareto_mixture_risk, pareto_risk

p = .01
components = [pareto_risk(a, p) for a in (1.2, 2.8)]
rows = {
    "mean exponent": pareto_risk(2, p),
    "average model risk": {k: sum(r[k] for r in components)/2 for k in ("var", "es")},
    "predictive mixture": pareto_mixture_risk([1.2, 2.8], [.5, .5], p),
}
for name, r in rows.items():
    print(f"{name}: VaR={r['var']:.2f}, ES={r['es']:.2f}")

Output

mean exponent: VaR=10.00, ES=20.00
average model risk: VaR=25.80, ES=143.28
predictive mixture: VaR=26.17, ES=156.38

Estimation adds another source of uncertainty¶

The Hill estimator estimates the extreme-value index ξ=1/α\xi=1/\alphaξ=1/α from a chosen number kkk of upper log spacings. Threshold choice and finite-sample error are additional assumptions. In an exact Pareto model the fixed-kkk reciprocal estimate is biased; Jensen at its mean therefore does not by itself compare its plug-in risk to the true risk. Nor does a distribution of repeated fitted parameters automatically become a posterior mixture for future losses.

The example reuses hill_alpha_estimator and pareto_risk. It uses a known synthetic cutoff of one, so it isolates exponent error instead of estimating the cutoff as well. At every kkk, it retains fits with infinite ES. The intervals summarize sampling variation; they are not confidence intervals.

Repeated fixed-k estimates
import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.estimators import hill_alpha_estimator
from xmath.incerto.risk_measures import pareto_risk

rng = np.random.default_rng(1307)
samples = 1 + rng.pareto(1.2, (400, 250))
for k in (25, 100):
    alphas = [hill_alpha_estimator(x, k) for x in samples]
    risks = [pareto_risk(a, .01) for a in alphas]
    lo, mid, hi = np.quantile([r['var'] for r in risks], [.1, .5, .9])
    infinite = sum(np.isinf(r['es']) for r in risks)
    print(f"k={k}: VaR 10/50/90%={lo:.1f}/{mid:.1f}/{hi:.1f}; infinite ES={infinite}/400")

Output

k=25: VaR 10/50/90%=16.9/45.4/131.3; infinite ES=66/400
k=100: VaR 10/50/90%=29.6/46.4/76.3; infinite ES=13/400

At k=400k=400k=400, 0 of 2,000 fits have infinite ES, a finite-sample count that does not establish zero population probability; the rule of three gives an approximate one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of 3/2000=0.15%3/2000=0.15\%3/2000=0.15%.

The same moment distinction applies to direct sample ES: observations can yield a finite numerical average even when the population ES is infinite. The point-forecast evaluation and plug-in mean pages explain the related loss-moment and boundary problems.

Sources and reproduction¶

The definitions, finite counterexample, ES subadditivity, Pareto formulas, and common-cutoff uncertainty comparisons are proved above. Chapter 13 supplies the error-propagation context; it is not cited as a proof of every extension here. The two figures are generated by uv run python demos/incerto/probability_conflation.py, through the shared figure style and exporter. No observed financial data or investment performance claim enters the examples.
